awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I: Scaling Up Tunable High-Frequency Microwave Heating for Pharmaceutical and Biologics Manufacturing
awd_abstract_narration:
This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project will result in fundamental knowledge needed to solve the scale-up problem for fast, uniform, volumetric heating during manufacturing of freeze-dried medicines, diagnostics, preservative-free foods, and other high-value sensitive materials. The findings will facilitate a significant improvement in manufacturing capacity for most freeze-dried goods and ultimately provide a pathway towards addressing recurring shortages and securing long-term availability. This SBIR research will produce data critical for process understanding as well as new quality control methodologies necessary for regulatory acceptance of microwave drying. The technology will be initially marketed to research and development units or organizations having a clear and viable downstream pathway towards manufacturing. The key competitive advantages offered by the technology are its ability to be noninvasively retrofitted to both new and legacy freeze-drying systems and its capability of producing uniform high-frequency electromagnetic fields specifically targeted towards frozen materials.

This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project aims to improve manufacturing performance of high-value freeze-dried materials having limited shelf life using high-frequency microwave heating. The overall goal of the project is to gain the fundamental knowledge required to effectively scale the technology from laboratory to large-volume manufacturing freeze-drying systems. Key research objectives to be addressed include developing new experimental methods for estimating the effective dielectric properties of frozen aqueous solutions and primary packaging, identifying appropriate physics-based models and parameters for system modeling, and implementing model-based closed-loop control strategies to drive the freeze-drying process at optimal rates. To accomplish these tasks, multiple microwave sources will be fabricated and installed on a modified laboratory freeze-dryer together with a suite of temperature sensing technologies. Experimental measurements will provide the data necessary to develop the coupled unsteady electromagnetic and heat and mass transfer simulations for identifying the scale-up characteristics, microwave source interaction, and volumetric heating performance. Free radical production in the vacuum environment and material compatibility with the electric fields over the system bandwidth will also be assessed either explicitly using appropriate probes or implicitly via bioindicators.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Lyophilization, commonly known as freeze drying, is the gold standard for stabilizing sensitive vaccines, injectable biologics, diagnostic reagents, and preservative-free foods prior to long-term storage. The process can extend shelf life from days to years and reduces dependence on costly and complicated cold-chain logistics. However, lyophilization is slow and expensive, often taking days or even weeks to complete. Our current production capacity, together with the surging demand for novel injectable biologics, is causing recurring shortages for critical life-saving medicines. Expanding our domestic lyophilization capacity is critical to securing the pharmaceutical supply chain.

This NSF SBIR Phase I project aimed to develop a tunable high-frequency microwave heating system that could safely and effectively accelerate the lyophilization process for injectable drugs and biologics. The LyoWave team achieved this goal by successfully designing, building, and testing a new platform known as TurboDryTM. The unique technology is designed to retrofit directly to existing lyophilization systems with minimal modification and integrate with industry-standard control and data management protocols. The project produced four principal outcomes:

First, two fully integrated solid-state TurboDryTM sources were built, installed, and tested on a laboratory lyophilizer. Benchmarking experiments with real and model pharmaceutical API demonstrated that microwave heating reduced cycle times by 30 to 50 percent compared to the conventional process across multiple product types, dosage forms, and packaging configurations. Downstream analytical testing following these experiments indicated no statistically significant differences in any standard critical product quality attributes.

Second, computational electromagnetic and thermal models at frequencies between 13.75-14.25 GHz were developed and validated to predict heating uniformity and product temperature response inside the lyophilization chamber. Simulations confirmed that the electromagnetic mixing approach achieves approximately 2.5 times greater heating uniformity than fixed-frequency microwave systems, and the thermal model agreed with experimental measurements to within 2 degrees Celsius.

Third, a new waveguide-based method was developed for measuring the complex permittivity, a fundamental electrical property describing the responsiveness of a material to microwave energy, of frozen pharmaceutical systems at controlled temperatures between -25 and 40 degrees Celsius. This measurement capability did not previously exist for the materials and frequency range relevant to freeze drying and produced the first published dataset of dielectric properties for common pharmaceutical excipients in the frozen state above 10 GHz.

Fourth, closed-loop temperature control of the product was demonstrated during drying, with the system automatically adjusting microwave power in real time based on feedback from temperature sensors. This represents a departure from the open-loop control strategies used universally in industrial freeze drying today and has the potential to shorten cycle development timelines for new formulations and increase manufacturing throughput.

Beyond advancing scientific knowledge, this project contributed to broader societal goals. The results of this research are being disseminated to industry stakeholders through conferences, webinars, and LyoWave's membership in LyoHUB, a national industry-led consortium for advancing science and technology of lyophilization. The project also provided experiential learning opportunities across engineering, computer science, and marketing disciplines for both undergraduate and graduate students at Purdue University. 

Once commercialized and scaled, TurboDryTM promises to significantly increase the throughput of existing freeze-drying infrastructure, helping to alleviate drug shortages and strengthen domestic manufacturing capacity for essential medicines and vaccines.
